title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning and Runbooks — Reference
author: Priya Singh
content:
Overview

Purpose: This document is the canonical SRE reference for defining service-level objectives (SLOs), managing error budgets, conducting capacity planning, running reliability initiatives, and authoring operational runbooks. It applies to all customer-facing inference services (hosted API, Dedicated, Private control plane) and to platform components that directly affect customer latency, availability, or correctness.

Scope: inference-gateway, model-serving, batch-router, kv-cache, auth-service, telemetry-ingest.

---

### 1. SLO and Error Budget policy

Intro: SLOs quantify customer-facing expectations and form the basis for error budgets. Error budgets drive prioritization between feature work and reliability work. The SRE team owns the SLO definitions in collaboration with product and service owners.

SLO types and examples:
- Availability (user-visible success rate): measured as successful responses / total requests, 30d rolling.
- Latency (tail and median): p50/p95/p99 for inference request end-to-end (API gateway -> response).
- Throughput (capacity targets): sustained requests per second under target latency SLO.
- Correctness (quality): model inference deterministic checks, integrity checks, and regression detection tied to evals.

Canonical SLO targets (examples):
| Service | SLO metric | Target | Measurement window | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| inference-gateway (hosted) | availability (200/2xx) | "99.95%" | 30d rolling | "platform-frontend" |
| model-serving (low-latency models) | p99 latency (end-to-end) | "< 250ms" | 30d rolling | "serving-runtime" |
| kv-cache | cache hit rate (prefix cache) | ">= 92%" | 30d rolling | "serving-runtime" |

SLO definition checklist (all SLOs must include):
1) Service owner and contact
2) Exact success criteria (HTTP codes, business logic pass/fail)
3) Measurement pipeline (metering, aggregation job, dashboards)
4) Alert thresholds (see alerting section)
5) Review cadence (quarterly)

Error budget policy:
- Error budget = 1 - SLO. For a 99.95% SLO over 30 days, monthly budget is 0.05% of minutes or requests.
- Burn rates and actions:
  - Normal: burn rate <= 1x -> continue regular deployments.
  - Elevated: 1x < burn rate <= 4x -> notify service owner, pause lower-priority launches, schedule deep-dive within 48 hours.
  - Critical: burn rate > 4x -> immediate mitigations: halt all feature rollouts, roll back risky changes, engage on-call, escalate to EM and product.
- Escalation owners: SRE on-call -> SRE manager -> Head of Platform.
- Enforcement cadence: automated checks run hourly; if error budget breach persists for 6 consecutive hours at >1x, runbook must be executed.

---

### 2. Capacity planning (process and templates)

Principles: plan for typical day (p50), peak day (p95), and burst capacity (p99+). Aim for 2x buffer above business-critical p99 throughput unless contractual SLA requires higher. Use cost-performance tradeoffs (batching, quantization) where appropriate.

Quarterly capacity planning process (owner: eng-sre + infra finance):
1) Data collection (by 10th of quarter): historical RPS, token counts, model mix, KV hit rates.
2) Forecasting (by 15th): 3-month projection with scenarios: base, +25%, +50%.
3) Resource mapping (by 20th): map forecast to GPU/CPU/RAM, HPA rules, queue depth.
4) Validation (by 25th): run stress tests + perf bench for worst-case payloads.
5) Commitment (by end of month): purchase/reserve Dedicated capacity or adjust autoscaling policies.

Capacity sizing formula (simplified):
- required_gpus = ceil(peak_tokens_per_sec * avg_token_latency_ms / (tokens_per_gpu_per_sec * 1000))
- tokens_per_gpu_per_sec derived from benchmark suite (see benchmarking-and-perf-suite).

Capacity thresholds and SLA mapping:
| Threshold | Condition | Action | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Green | headroom > 40% | no action | SRE |
| Yellow | headroom 15-40% | review scaling policies, enable burst autoscale | SRE + infra|
| Red | headroom < 15% or sustained | activate capacity runbook, request procurement | SRE manager + infra finance|

Runbook for planned capacity incidents (procurement lead time):
1) Re-evaluate routing policies to favor higher throughput model variants.
2) Temporarily increase batching window for non-interactive routes.
3) Engage sales/customer-success if QoS may be impacted for enterprise customers.
4) Execute reserved instance purchase or schedule maintenance window for scaling.

---

### 3. Reliability initiatives and prioritization

Goal: Turn SLO violations into prioritized engineering projects (reliability initiatives) with clear success metrics.

Initiative lifecycle:
- Trigger: recurring SLO breach, incident leading to major outage, or analysis shows trend risk.
- Intake: short PRD + expected regression in cost/latency/availability.
- T-shirt sizing and prioritization: use impact = (customers affected * severity) and effort = (engineer-weeks).
- Acceptance criteria: objective improvement on SLOs and regression tests.
- Measurement: compare 30d rolling SLO before/after and verify with synthetic tests.

Examples of initiatives:
- Prefill KV cache during scale-ups to reduce cold-start latency.
- Adaptive batching algorithm for bursty workloads.
- Improved autoscaling signals (use token throughput + queue depth).

Ownership and cadence: reliability initiatives are reviewed at the weekly Reliability Review meeting. Quarterly roadmap items must include SLO impact statement.

---

### 4. Incident review standards and postmortem expectations

Objective: every Sev2/Sev1 incident requires a post-incident review (PIR) documented in Confluence within 7 days. PIRs must be blameless and focus on systemic fixes.

Postmortem template (mandatory fields):
- Incident summary (one-paragraph)
- Timeline (UTC) with key events and page links to alerts/dashboards
- Impact (customer-visible effects, affected regions, % of requests)
- Root cause analysis (contributing factors)
- Mitigations performed during incident
- Long-term fixes and owners (with due dates)
- Lessons learned and monitoring improvements
- Detection and recovery metrics (MTTD, MTTR)

Severity definitions and required actions:
- Sev1 (platform down or major national/regional degradation): immediate conference bridge, notify Execs, PIR in 3 days.
- Sev2 (significant customer impact for subset): on-call + escalation, PIR in 7 days.
- Sev3 (minor customer impact): document incident in weekly SRE review if it repeats.

Review process: once PIR is filed, SRE manager assigns an action owner and tracks to completion in the reliability backlog. Actions not completed within 30 days are escalated in the monthly reliability review.

---

### 5. Operational tooling and observability standards

Required telemetry for all SRE-owned services:
- Request-level traces (sampled at 1% default; increase to 10% for new issues).
- Per-route latency histograms (p50/p95/p99) emitted to metrics backend (Prometheus/Thanos/Grafana).
- Error counters by code and business-failure type.
- Capacity metrics: GPU utilization, queue depth, tokens/sec, batch sizes.
- Synthetic checks: health-checks for each region, per-model inference smoke tests with known prompts, and continuous evals for quality regression.

Dashboards and alerts:
- Standard dashboard templates stored in dashboards-and-alerts: "SLO overview", "Capacity heatmap", "Top error types".
- Alerting policy must include: symptom alerts (for SLOs) + root-cause alerts (for internal metrics).
- Alert thresholds must align with SLOs and error budget policy. Example: p99 latency > SLO for 5m -> page on-call.

Operational playbooks (examples):
- High p99 latency -> check model-serving queue depth, batch sizes, GPU memory; if OOM suspected, look for recent model loads or increased batch size; rollback canary if recent model change.
- API 5xx spike -> inspect auth-service and inference-gateway logs, validate downstream model-serving health endpoints, and check TTLs on caches.

Tooling integrations (must be configured):
- Alertmanager + PagerDuty for paging.
- Grafana for dashboards.
- Tracing via Jaeger/Tempo.
- Long-term metrics in Thanos/BigQuery for SLO reporting.
- Incident management in Statuspage and Jira for follow-ups.

---

### 6. Runbook templates and examples

Runbook metadata (required):
- title, service, severity, on-call rota, runbook_last_tested (date), owner.

Example: Runbook — High inference p99 latency (severity: P1)
1) Page on-call and create incident in Statuspage.
2) Check SLO dashboard: confirm p99 breach window and affected regions.
3) Run quick diagnostics:
   - curl -sv "https://grafana.internal/api/metrics?query=p99_inference_latency{service=\"model-serving\"}"
   - kubectl -n serving get pods -o wide | grep model-serving
   - check GPU memory and process OOM logs: ssh node && nvidia-smi -q && journalctl -u model-serving | tail -n 200
4) If model-serving pod OOM or hung: restart pod, scale up replica count by +20% and monitor.
5) If recent deploy in last 30m: rollback to previous revision (CLI):
   - kubectl rollout undo deployment/model-serving -n serving
6) If issue persists > 15m: switch routing policy to fallback model-variant (route: batch-router -> variant-b).
7) After recovery: file PIR, tag incident with SLO impact and update runbook if steps were missing.

Runbook testing cadence: each runbook must be exercised at least once per quarter (game-day) and annotated with runbook_last_tested.

---

### 7. Governance, review, and ownership

- SLO review cadence: quarterly review with product and account managers.
- Runbook review: every 6 months or after any incident that touched the runbook.
- Audit: security/compliance will sample SLO definitions annually for regulated customers.
- Documentation ownership: SRE on-call leads maintain runbooks; eng leads maintain SLOs for their services.
